title: Ayushman Vay Vandana (AB PM-JAY for senior citizens aged 70 and above)
authority: National Health Authority, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
summary: Since 29 October 2024, AB PM-JAY gives free treatment benefits of up to Rs 5 lakh per year on a family basis to all senior citizens aged 70 and above, irrespective of their socio-economic status. The Health Benefit Package covers 1,961 procedures across 27 specialties at empanelled public and private hospitals.
applicabilityNote: For senior citizens in families already covered by AB PM-JAY, the source describes an additional top-up for the senior citizen. Check the source for how the cover is shared.

title: Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) and the Digital Health Incentive Scheme
authority: National Health Authority, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
summary: ABDM builds the national digital health infrastructure: the ABHA health account for patients, the Health Facility Registry (HFR) for facilities and the Healthcare Professionals Registry (HPR) for clinicians, with consent-based sharing of health records. Under the Digital Health Incentive Scheme (DHIS), effective from 1 January 2023, facilities registered on HFR can earn incentives of up to Rs 5 crore.
applicabilityNote: DHIS terms change through corrigenda that apply to set periods. Check the DHIS page for the corrigendum in force.

title: Janani Suraksha Yojana (JSY)
authority: National Health Mission, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
summary: A safe motherhood intervention under the National Health Mission that promotes institutional delivery among poor pregnant women through cash assistance, to reduce maternal and neonatal deaths. It gives a special dispensation to states with low institutional delivery rates, including Madhya Pradesh.
applicabilityNote: Cash amounts and who qualifies differ between low performing and high performing states. Check the source for current amounts.

title: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK)
authority: National Health Mission, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
summary: Launched in June 2011, JSSK entitles all pregnant women delivering in public health institutions to free delivery, including caesarean section, with free drugs and consumables, diagnostics, blood where required, diet and transport. Similar entitlements apply to sick newborns and infants up to one year of age treated in public health institutions.
applicabilityNote: Applies to public health institutions, not private hospitals.

title: Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA)
authority: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
summary: Launched on 9 June 2016, PMSMA gives free, comprehensive antenatal care on the 9th of every month at designated government health facilities, for pregnant women in the second or third trimester, with a focus on finding high-risk pregnancies early. Obstetricians, radiologists and physicians from the private sector can volunteer to provide services on these days.
applicabilityNote: Private doctors take part as volunteers by registering on the PMSMA portal.

title: Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (nutrition support for TB patients)
authority: Central TB Division, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
summary: All TB patients receive nutrition support of Rs 1,000 per month for the entire duration of treatment, paid by direct benefit transfer. The amount was increased from Rs 500 per month, as announced on 7 October 2024.

title: Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK)
authority: National Health Mission, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
summary: RBSK screens children from birth to 18 years of age for the four Ds: defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and development delays, spanning 32 common health conditions, for early detection and free treatment and management, including surgeries.

title: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and DPDP Rules, 2025
authority: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
summary: A hospital that processes patients' personal data is a Data Fiduciary. It must give a separate, clear consent notice explaining the specific purpose, let people withdraw consent, keep reasonable security safeguards, and inform affected individuals of a personal data breach without delay. The Rules, notified in November 2025, give an eighteen-month period for phased compliance. Penalties go up to Rs 250 crore for failing to keep security safeguards.
applicabilityNote: Significant Data Fiduciaries have extra duties such as audits and impact assessments. Check the notified Rules for the dates that apply to each provision.

title: Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016: authorisation in Madhya Pradesh
summary: MPPCB grants authorisation under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016. Its list of required documents includes the membership certificate of a common bio-medical waste treatment facility and, for renewal or expansion, a point-wise compliance report on the authorisation conditions and the Form IV annual report.
applicabilityNote: Validity differs for bedded and non-bedded facilities under the Rules. Check the Rules and MPPCB before relying on a period.

title: Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate under the Water and Air Acts (Madhya Pradesh)
summary: MPPCB grants Consent to Establish and Consent to Operate, and their renewal, under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981. MPPCB lists the documents required for each consent on its website.
applicabilityNote: The source does not give the validity period or category for hospitals. These are stated in each consent order.

title: AERB licence or registration for diagnostic X-ray equipment
summary: Hospitals and diagnostic X-ray centres must obtain a licence or registration from AERB, applied for online through eLORA. The licence is valid for five years from the date of issue. Every X-ray department must have a Radiation Safety Officer, and routine quality assurance tests are done once in two years.
applicabilityNote: CT and interventional radiology have extra requirements. Check eLORA for the current guidelines.

title: Licence to operate a blood centre (Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945)
authority: Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) and the State Licensing Authority
summary: A licence is required to run a blood bank; running one without a licence is an offence under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. The application for grant or renewal is made on Form 27-C, the licence is issued on Form 28-C and renewal on Form 26-G. A licence is valid for five years from the date it is granted or renewed. The fee to open a blood bank is Rs 7,500.
applicabilityNote: Blood storage centres in hospitals follow separate guidelines with a different validity. Check the source for the type of facility.

title: NABH Entry-Level Certification Programme (2nd Edition)
authority: National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH), Quality Council of India
summary: A single entry-level quality framework for small healthcare organisations (up to 50 beds) and hospitals (51 beds and above). Standards are grouped into Core, Commitment and Excellence, applied step by step over the first assessment and later renewals. A hospital must have been functional for at least six months and meet minimum bed occupancy to apply.
applicabilityNote: This is a voluntary certification, not a licence. Check the NABH page for current validity and renewal timelines.

title: Reporting foreign patients on Form III (Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025)
authority: Bureau of Immigration, Ministry of Home Affairs
summary: Every hospital, nursing home or medical institution providing medical, lodging or sleeping facility must record the particulars of every foreigner taking indoor treatment, including OCI cardholders, and send Form III (formerly Form C) on the e-FRRO portal within twenty-four hours of arrival, and the departure details within twenty-four hours of departure. Records are kept electronically for one year, and the birth or death of a foreigner is reported within seven days.
applicabilityNote: Penalties under the Act range from Rs 10,000 to Rs 3 lakh per offence.
